Its exact reference—meaning which person is intended—depends on the surrounding passage, since the same name occurs in more than one setting.

This Hebrew word expresses “up,” functioning with a verb to mark the direction or completion of an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in passages from 2 Kings, Nehemiah, Isaiah, and Amos. Its precise force in any sentence depends on the surrounding words, since the Hebrew verb and this accompanying element work together. The word is therefore best understood as a verbal particle contributing the sense “up” to the action being described.

This Hebrew word means “summer,” referring to the warm season of the year. It functions as a word describing a seasonal time, rather than an action, person, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Isaiah 18:6. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic reference remains the season called “summer.”

Keziz is a Hebrew proper name, rendered “Keziz.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 18:21, so its ordinary use is limited to that single occurrence. The wording preserves it as a name rather than translating it as a descriptive term; its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “destruction,” referring to ruin or the bringing down of something. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible’s Old Testament corpus, at Jeremiah 46:20. The word’s basic sense points to a destructive outcome rather than to a person, place, or action of restoration. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the idea of destruction or ruin.

This word means “trembling,” describing the physical act or condition of shaking with fear, distress, or weakness. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 12:18. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that verse must be understood from its context; the word itself points plainly to trembling rather than calm or steadiness.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “oath”: a solemn spoken commitment or sworn promise. It is used for an oath that a person makes, keeps, or is bound by. In the Old Testament, the word can appear in settings involving promises, commands, giving, and speech, showing that an oath carries serious responsibility rather than being a casual statement. It occurs 30 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, emphasizing a recurring scriptural concern with truthful commitments before God and other people.

e.t: This Hebrew word expresses having or reaching enough—being supplied or filled to a sufficient degree. In ordinary use, it functions as a supporting idea within a sentence rather than naming a person or object. Its six Old Testament occurrences are found in Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Haggai, where the surrounding wording determines whether the sense concerns having something, being satisfied, or becoming full. The central idea remains sufficiency: something reaches the amount needed or desired. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to something designated as “principal”—the foremost or primary part within an arrangement. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs only once, at Isaiah 28:25, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The available rendering supports the idea of something holding the leading place, but the word’s broader use cannot be established from additional occurrences.

e.t: This Hebrew word expresses “most,” marking something as extreme or especially intense. It functions as an intensifying word rather than naming a person, place, or object. In its three Old Testament occurrences, it serves as the object of what is spoken or described, showing that the word identifies the heightened degree of a matter. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Bul refers to the eighth month in the Hebrew calendar. It is a month name rather than a general description, and this word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 1 Kings 6:38. The passage associates Bul with the completion of the temple’s building work, but the word itself identifies the time of year. English Bible renderings preserve the name “Bul” and also identify it as “eighth.”
